subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Salmonella are gram‑negative rods that invade the intestinal mucosa and can cause a spectrum from self‑limited gastroenteritis to life‑threatening typhoid fever. Host factors such as gastric acidity and immune status determine severity.

sections.p: Salmonella are facultative intracellular, motile, gram‑negative bacilli transmitted via contaminated food, water, or animal contact. They belong to the Enterobacteriaceae family and have many serovars, the most important being Typhi (typhoid fever) and non‑typhoidal serovars (food‑borne gastroenteritis).
b: Facultative intracellular → survives in macrophages
Motile via peritrichous flagella
Acid‑labile; gastric acid is key defense

sections.p: Salmonella possess lipopolysaccharide (LPS) with O‑antigen, H‑antigen flagellar protein, and Vi capsule (Typhi). They use type III secretion systems to invade M cells and replicate within phagocytes.
b: Vi capsule protects Typhi from opsonisation
Type III secretion injects effectors into host cells
Non‑typhoidal strains lack Vi capsule

sections.p: Ingestion of contaminated food/water leads to gastric passage, invasion of ileal Peyer’s patches, and systemic spread via lymphatics. Typhoid can become chronic carrier state in gallbladder.
b: Incubation: 6–72 h (non‑typhoidal), 6–30 days (Typhi)
Carrier state common after Typhi infection

sections.p: Non‑typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) usually cause self‑limited watery or bloody diarrhea; severe disease occurs in immunocompromised, sickle‑cell, or HIV patients. Salmonella Typhi causes systemic febrile illness with rose spots, abdominal pain, and possible intestinal perforation.
b: NTS: mild gastroenteritis, may cause bacteremia in high‑risk hosts
Typhoid: stepwise fever, hepatosplenomegaly, intestinal ulceration
Complications: septic arthritis (sickle cell), osteomyelitis, meningitis

sections.p: Diagnosis relies on stool culture for NTS and blood culture for Typhi; serology (Widal) is unreliable. In low‑resource settings, stool microscopy and clinical criteria are used.
b: Culture: gold standard, 48‑72 h for growth
PCR: rapid but often unavailable

t.b: Identifies non‑typhoidal infection; positive growth confirms diagnosis
Detects Salmonella Typhi bacteremia; positive result guides systemic therapy
Detects anti‑O/anti‑H antibodies; positive may suggest Typhi but many false‑positives, use only when culture unavailable

sections.p: Mild NTS gastroenteritis needs only rehydration; antibiotics reserved for high‑risk patients. Typhoid requires systemic antibiotics. Public health measures focus on safe water, food hygiene, and vaccination.
b: Rehydration: oral rehydration salts or IV fluids
Antibiotics for NTS: fluoroquinolones or third‑gen cephalosporins in severe cases
Typhoid: ceftriaxone or azithromycin; avoid fluoroquinolones where resistance high
Vaccines: oral Ty21a, injectable Vi polysaccharide

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams.
b: Acid suppression (PPIs) increases risk of Salmonella infection
Sickle‑cell patients with Salmonella septic arthritis need joint aspiration
Typhoid fever incubation is longer than most food‑borne diarrheas

whenToSeekHelp: High fever >39 °C with abdominal pain and vomiting
Persistent diarrhea >7 days, blood in stool, or fever in immunocompromised

faq.q: Why are infants less susceptible to non‑typhoidal Salmonella enteritis?
faq.a: Maternal antibodies and limited exposure to contaminated foods protect infants.

faq.q: What is the most important host defense against Salmonella dysentery?
faq.a: Stomach acid; low pH kills most organisms before they reach the intestine.

faq.q: How long after exposure does Salmonella Typhi typically cause symptoms?

exam: Describe the pathogenesis of Salmonella Typhi and why it can become a chronic carrier.
List the first‑line antibiotics for severe non‑typhoidal Salmonella infection in a patient with sickle‑cell disease and justify your choice.
Explain how gastric acid suppression predisposes to Salmonella infection and how this influences clinical management.
